title: The knight: the piece that jumps
outcomes: Taps every square a knight can jump to, including captures
Knows the knight is not blocked by pieces in between, unlike rooks and bishops
Tells which pieces can reach a square when nobody names the piece
Says why a knight in the corner has fewer choices than one in the centre
Finds the first jump of a two-jump route
Names the exceptions to 'only the landing square counts': a pinned knight, and a king in check
Uses the colour switch to rule out impossible routes
Explains to a friend how a knight moves and why it differs from a bishop

steps.text: The knight is the piece beginners most often misjudge. A rook or bishop travels along a line the eye can follow, but a knight's jump leaves no line to follow [I]. By the end you should be able to explain to a friend how to find every square a knight can reach, and why it is not like a bishop. First, try one.

That was a knight move. The knight travels in an **L**: two squares straight, then one square to the side. The next board shows all eight of its jumps from near the middle of the board. Look at where each one lands before you read on.

steps.caption: From a central square the knight has eight places to land. Each is two squares one way and one square at a right angle.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 has exactly these eight landing squares.

steps.caption: A picture that may help: every jump joins opposite corners of a rectangle two squares by three. Here it runs from d4 to e6. [V] That is exact geometry, checked for every knight move; only how much it helps you is a guess [H].

line.say: Two squares up and one across: the knight lands at the far corner of the shaded rectangle.

claims.statement: The knight can jump from d4 to e6.

steps.caption: Lying on its side, the rectangle is three squares wide and two tall. The jump is the same L turned a quarter.

line.say: Two squares across and one up: the same shape turned on its side.

claims.statement: The knight can jump from d4 to f5.

steps.caption: Watch the colour of the square under the knight. It changes with every jump: dark, light, dark. A landing square never has the colour of the square the knight left. [V] Checked for every square on the board: no knight jump keeps its colour.

line.say: From the dark square d4 the knight lands on a light square, e6.
From the light square e6 it lands on a dark square, f4.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 has eight landing squares.

steps.text: **Colour switch [V].** Every jump lands on the opposite colour, so the colour works as a counter. One jump, three jumps, any odd number: the other colour. Two jumps, four jumps: back to the starting colour. Before you plan a route, check the colour of the target. If the count cannot match, no route exists.

steps.caption: At the start of a game the rook and bishop have no free square, but the knights can already leave. Jumping over the pawns in front is allowed.

line.say: The knight jumps over the pawns in front of it and lands on f3.
Black's knight does the same on its side.
The other knight comes out too.

claims.statement: The knight on b1 can go to a3 and c3.
The knight on g1 can go to f3 and h3.
The rook on a1 has no move.
The bishop on c1 has no move.

steps.text: A rook, bishop or queen slides, so every square on its path must be empty. A knight does not slide. It leaves one square and appears on another, so pieces in between never matter. Only the **landing square** counts. It must not hold one of your own pieces, and the move must not leave your own king in check.

steps.title: A crowd does not stop a knight
steps.prompt: At the start, pawns stand in front of every piece. Predict first: can the knight on b1 move? Can the bishop on c1?

steps.caption: The landing square decides. Own pawns on c2 and e2 block those two jumps. Enemy pieces on b5, e6 and f5 can be captured, which means taken off the board.

line.say: The knight lands on e6 and takes the bishop. Landing on an enemy piece is a capture.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 can go to exactly six squares: c2 and e2 hold its own pawns.

steps.caption: The knight on e2 is pinned. If it jumped away, the rook would give check along the file, so it has no legal move at all, even though its landing squares are empty.

claims.statement: The pinned knight on e2 has no legal move.

steps.caption: In a corner the knight has only two landing squares. Every other jump would leave the board.

claims.statement: The knight on a1 can go to b3 and c2 only.

steps.caption: On the edge it has four. One jump back toward the middle gives it more room.

line.say: The jump to c4 takes the knight toward the middle, where it can choose among more squares.

claims.statement: The knight on a3 can go to b1, b5, c2 and c4.

steps.text: **Counting jumps [V]:** a corner gives 2, other edge squares 3 or 4, the ring one step in 4 or 6, and the sixteen central squares 8. The reason: jumps that would leave the board are lost, and the nearer the edge the more are lost. **[R]** Old saying: a knight on the rim is dim. **[H]** It usually does less there, but a plan can justify it.

steps.caption: Reaching b5 from b1 takes two jumps. The first can be a3 or c3: either is an L away from b5. Pick the first square so that the target is one jump from it.

line.say: First jump: to a3, an L away from b5.

claims.statement: The knight on b1 can go to a3, c3 or d2.
After b1 to a3 the knight reaches b5.
After b1 to c3 the knight reaches b5.
After b1 to d2 the knight does not reach b5.

steps.text: Jumps work both ways. If a knight can go from d2 to e4, it can go from e4 back to d2. So to find which knights can reach a square, picture a knight standing on that square and look at its eight landing squares. A knight on any of them can get there.

steps.caption: Who can reach e4? The knight on d2 (it stands on one of e4's eight L-squares), the bishop on b1 along the diagonal and the rook on h4 along the rank. The knight on e2 is two squares straight below, which is not an L.

line.say: The knight on d2 lands on e4, one of the eight squares around it.

claims.statement: Exactly three white pieces reach e4.
The knight on d2 can jump to e4.
The bishop on b1 can slide to e4.
The rook on h4 can slide to e4.
The knight on e2 cannot reach e4.

steps.text: **Two blind spots.** A bishop's check can be answered by putting a piece in between. A knight's check cannot: nothing can stand in a jump. You must move the king or take the knight. That is why a knight check is hard to meet.

steps.caption: The bishop on b5 checks along the diagonal. Black can block with the knight, on c6 or d7, besides moving the king.

claims.statement: Black is in check from the bishop.
Black can block on c6.
Black can block on d7.

steps.caption: The knight on g6 checks the king on h8. Nothing can be put in between, and the only legal answers are the three king moves.

claims.statement: Black is in check from the knight.
Black has exactly three legal moves, all by the king.

steps.text: **Why a knight is different from a bishop.** Its attack cannot be blocked. It can hit two pieces in one jump, a fork. By convention [R] it is worth about three pawns, like a bishop. Because every jump changes colour, it reaches squares a bishop never can.

steps.caption: The knight jumps to d6 with check and attacks the rook on b7 as well. The king must move, and the rook falls.

line.say: Check, and the rook on b7 is attacked too.

claims.statement: The knight can jump to d6.
The fork wins the rook.

steps.text: **[H] A conjecture, not a rule:** knights tend to do best when pawns clog the centre, because a jump ignores the pawns in the way, while bishops tend to prefer open boards. No coach's view was used for this. Treat it as a hunch to test in your own games, and note when it fails.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend who has never seen a knight how to find all its landing squares, and why a crowd around it does not matter. Write it in your own words first. Then tick what you included.

fields.label: The L shape: two squares one way, one to the side
It jumps, so pieces in between do not matter
An own piece on the landing square blocks it; an enemy piece can be taken
Edges and corners leave fewer squares
Every jump switches the square colour

steps.text: **A model answer, to compare with yours.** The knight moves in an L: two squares one way and one to the side. To list its landing squares, test all eight, cross off any that leave the board or hold your own piece. A crowd in between does not matter, because it jumps. Near an edge fewer jumps stay on the board, and every jump changes the colour of its square.
